film.title: How Do Plants Respond?
film.bigQuestion: If a plant can't move from place to place, how does it still survive when things change around it?

captions.text: Tick, tock. A plant can never walk away.
In Fort Myers, Florida, one giant tree spreads out like a whole forest.
Look up. Long roots hang down from its branches.
They grow down until they touch the ground. Then they become new trunks.
Now tip a young plant on its side. What will it do?
Its stems curve back up, toward the sky.
Plants can't move. So how do they know which way to grow?

words: A change in the way a living thing grows or acts because of something around it.
Everything around a living thing: air, water, soil, light, and other living things.
Something in the environment that causes a living thing to respond. Light, water, gravity, and heat are stimuli for plants.
The force that pulls everything toward the ground. Plants use it to know which way is down.
When a plant stem or leaf grows toward light. "Photo" means light and "tropism" means turning.
Staying alive and continuing to grow. Plant responses help plants get what they need to survive.
When roots grow down and stems grow up because of gravity. "Gravi" means gravity, "tropism" means turning.
When roots grow toward water. "Hydro" means water, "tropism" means turning.

parts.title: Plants Can't Walk, But They Respond
parts.html:
A plant can't walk toward water or away from the dark. But it still responds to the world around it, by changing how it grows.

Something in the environment that a plant responds to is called a stimulus. The change in how it grows is a response. The plant isn't choosing. Its cells just grow faster on one side, so it bends.

parts.title: Light and Water
parts.html:
Stems and leaves grow toward light. This is phototropism. A plant by a window slowly leans toward the glass, so its leaves catch more sunlight to make food.

Roots grow toward water in the soil. This is hydrotropism. It helps the plant get the water it needs to stay alive.

parts.title: Gravity and Heat
parts.html:
Roots grow down and stems grow up, no matter which way a seed is planted. This response to gravity is called gravitropism. It keeps roots in the soil and leaves in the light.

Plants respond to heat, too. When it turns cold, many trees drop their leaves to save water and energy. When spring warmth returns, buds open and growing starts again.

check.q: The seed was planted upside down. Why did its root still end up growing down?

options.ok: Yes! Roots respond to gravity, so they grow down no matter which way the seed was planted.

compare.title: Which part grows toward light, and which grows toward water?
compare.look: Two parts of real young plants, each on a lit specimen tray. Specimen A is a bean plant's stem and leaves. Specimen B is a young plant's roots, growing in soil. Under the trays are two things for a test: a desk lamp and a wet sponge.

compare.testDo: Put the desk lamp beside one tray and the wet sponge beside the other: drag them, or tap each one, then tap a tray. Press Let 3 days pass. Then swap them and press it again.
compare.disclaimer: This is a model. Real plants take days to bend, so the page shows what scientists see, sped up.

Alamp.text: After 3 days, the stem bent toward the lamp, and the leaves turned to face the light.

Asponge.text: The stem didn't bend toward the wet sponge. Stems reach for light, not water. Try the lamp here.

Bsponge.text: After 3 days, the roots grew toward the wet sponge, where the soil was wetter.

Blamp.text: The roots didn't grow toward the lamp. Under the ground, roots head down and toward water. Try the sponge here.

compare.frame: This plant part ___, so it grows toward ___.

curator.A: Stem with leaves → grows toward light. This is phototropism. Leaves that face the light catch more sunlight to make food.
curator.B: Roots in the soil → grow toward water. This is hydrotropism. Roots that reach wet soil get the water the plant needs.

after.alt: An old drawing of a machine that holds a small plant sideways and slowly turns it around
after.html: Over 100 years ago, scientists built this machine, called a clinostat. It slowly turns a plant around and around, so gravity pulls on every side of it. On the machine, the plant can't tell which way is down. That helped scientists prove that plants use gravity to know down from up.

wall.title: Ride down Edison's banyan, from leaves to roots
wall.look: A cutaway (a slice) of a giant banyan tree, from its sunny leaves at the top down to its roots under the ground. It is a model. Each level is one part of the tree, and each part responds to something different. The brass dial on the left shows which part you are at.
wall.do: First, make a prediction. Then brush the glowing layer: drag across it (or tap it again and again) until the plant shows.

predict.q: Which way do you think the banyan's hanging roots grow?
predict.mine: Your prediction: {p}. Let's ride down the tree and find out.
predict.confirm: You predicted the hanging roots grow down. The evidence agrees: they grow down until they reach the ground.
predict.change: You predicted the hanging roots grow up. The evidence changed that idea: they grow down, toward the ground, because of gravity.

wall.skyAlt: A giant banyan tree with many trunks and one huge canopy
wall.skyCap: Edison's banyan · Edison & Ford Winter Estates, Fort Myers, Florida
wall.locked: Brush the level above first. The elevator goes down, one level at a time.
wall.first: Brush the glowing top layer. Drag across it (or tap it again and again).
wall.next: Going down the tree. Brush Level {n}.
wall.endText: Look at the line. The leaves at the top grow toward light. The roots below grow down with gravity and toward water. The root trunks hold the giant tree up.
wall.rule: Every part of a plant responds to its environment. Leaves grow toward light, roots grow down with gravity, and roots grow toward water. These responses help the plant survive.

mix.q: A banyan's hanging roots grow down, even up in the air. Why?

options.t: They are heavy, so they flop down.
options.miss: Not quite. Thin roots aren't heavy, and the tip keeps growing down on purpose. What pulls everything toward the ground?

options.t: They respond to gravity, so they grow down.
options.ok: Yes! Roots respond to gravity. That's gravitropism, and it leads the banyan's roots all the way to the soil.

wow.title: Sunflowers that follow the sun
wow.alt: A huge field of sunflowers under a misty morning sky
wow.caption: A sunflower field on a misty morning.
wow.html:
Young sunflowers face east at sunrise. All day long, their heads slowly turn west, following the sun across the sky.

At night, they swing back to face east again, ready for morning! When a sunflower grows up and blooms, it stops turning and faces east.
wow.insetCap: A grown-up sunflower in bloom, facing the morning sun.

keyIdea: Plants respond to light, water, gravity, and heat by changing how and when they grow. These responses help them get what they need to survive, even though they can never move from place to place.

options.ok: 🌱 That's right! No matter which way the seed was planted, the roots grow down and the stem grows up because of gravity.

quiz.q: Why do plant responses, like growing toward light, help a plant survive?

options.t: They make the plant grow faster than other plants
options.miss: Plants can't move from place to place, but they can grow differently. Which answer connects the response to getting something the plant needs?

options.t: They help the plant move to a better place
options.miss: Plants can't move from place to place, but they can grow differently. Which answer connects the response to getting something the plant needs?

options.t: They help the plant get what it needs, like sunlight and water
options.ok: ⭐ Exactly! Each response helps the plant find or reach something it needs: light for food, water to stay alive, and soil for support.

partA.title: Match the response

items.q: A stem curves toward the window over three weeks. What is the stimulus, and what is the response called?

options.ok: Yes. The stem responded to light from the window. That's phototropism.

options.miss: The stem bent sideways, toward the window. What comes through a window?
Stems bend toward light, not water. What comes through a window?

items.q: A seedling's roots grew straight down, even though the seed was planted on its side. What stimulus caused this?

options.miss: The roots grew straight down, not toward water. What pulls everything down?

options.ok: Yes. The roots responded to gravity. That's gravitropism.

options.miss: Roots are under the ground, away from light. What pulls everything down?

items.q: Roots in a dry garden grew toward a leaky pipe buried in the soil. What were they responding to?

options.miss: There's no light under the ground. What comes out of a leaky pipe?
The roots grew sideways, toward the pipe. What comes out of a leaky pipe?

options.ok: Yes. The roots responded to water from the leaky pipe. That's hydrotropism.
